hints: Focus on how HBr adds to an alkene, the electrophile $H^+$ attacks the $C=C$ double bond first to make a positive ion.
Adding $H^+$ to $CH_3CH=CH_2$ can give either a secondary carbocation on the middle carbon or a primary carbocation on the end carbon.
Recall that alkyl groups stabilise a positive charge, so compare the stability of the two possible carbocations to see which forms fastest and in greatest amount.
walkthrough:
**Recall the mechanism type**

Electrophilic addition starts when the electron-rich pi bond of propene attracts the electrophile, $H^+$ from $HBr$. This forms a carbocation intermediate, then $Br^-$ attacks in step 2.

$$CH_3CH=CH_2 + H^+ \rightarrow \text{carbocation intermediate}$$

**Draw the two possible carbocations**

If $H^+$ adds to the end $CH_2$ carbon, you get $CH_3CH^+CH_3$, a secondary carbocation. If $H^+$ adds to the middle $CH$ carbon, you get $CH_3CH_2CH_2^+$, a primary carbocation.

**Apply carbocation stability and Markovnikov**

Secondary carbocations are more stable than primary ones because the two methyl groups donate electron density by the inductive effect. The more stable intermediate forms faster and in greater amount, so the major route is via $CH_3CH^+CH_3$.

options.A: Correct. $CH_3CH^+CH_3$ is the secondary carbocation formed when $H^+$ adds to the terminal carbon. It is stabilised by two alkyl groups, so it is much more stable than the primary alternative and forms in the greatest amount, leading to the Markovnikov product $CH_3CHBrCH_3$.
options.B: Incorrect. $CH_3CH_2CH_2^+$ is the primary carbocation formed when $H^+$ adds to the middle carbon. It has only one alkyl group stabilising the charge, so it is less stable, forms more slowly, and gives only a trace of product.
options.C: Incorrect. $CH_3CH^-CH_2Br$ is a carbanion (negative ion). Electrophilic addition does not make negative intermediates from the alkene, the pi bond is attacked by $H^+$, not by $Br^-$, so a negative charge on carbon is not formed.
options.D: Incorrect. $CH_3CHBrCH_2^-$ is also a carbanion. This reverses the mechanism by suggesting $Br$ adds first. In reality $H^+$ is the electrophile that adds first, so no carbanion intermediate is involved.
